title: Global and Local Stressors Cause the Decline of a Coral Reef in a No-Take Marine Protected Area
content: Coral reefs face increasing climate and local pressures, increasing reliance on marine protected areas (MPAs). However, evidence on MPA resilience against cumulative disturbances is limited. Pigeon Island Marine National Park (PIMNP), a no-take MPA in Sri Lanka, offers a natural experiment, having experienced local and global stressors. Local stressors are crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) outbreaks, macroalgal proliferation, and tourism pressure, while the global sea surface temperature increase caused coral bleaching. Benthic cover (line intercept transects) and reef fish communities (timed swim visual census) were compared across 2013, 2019, and 2025 using univariate, multivariate and correlation analyses. Live coral cover was approximately 43 % in 2013 and 2019, but declined to 15.1 % in 2025, while dead coral increased to 51.5 %, likely reflecting the 2023–2024 mass bleaching event. Cyanobacteriosponge Terpios hoshinota was first recorded at PIMNP in 2025 (1.8 % cover). Fish abundance and richness declined between 2013 and 2019, and community composition shifted (p < 0.001). Corallivores declined by 2025, tracking live coral loss (Spearman ρ = 0.597, p < 0.001), while detritivores and invertebrate-and-fish feeders increased with expanding dead substrate. These findings suggest MPA status alone did not prevent reef decline once thermal stress compounded pre-existing pressures.
